meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Education is the kindling of a flame, not the filling of a vessel'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Socrates. The idea is Plutarch's, from Moralia; the popular wording is a modern paraphrase first pinned on Socrates in 1966.

answer.label: Not Socrates — the idea is Plutarch’s
answer.authorDates: c. 46 – after 119 AD · Greek historian, biographer & philosopher
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Socrates ever said this. The thought comes from Plutarch, who wrote in his Moralia essay “On Listening to Lectures” that the mind “is not a vessel that needs filling, but wood that needs igniting.” The neat modern wording — “the kindling of a flame, not the filling of a vessel” — is a 20th-century paraphrase, and it was first attached to Socrates only in 1966, per Quote Investigator.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: Modern paraphrase; first credited to Socrates in 1966

source.excerpt: For the mind does not require filling like a bottle, but rather, like wood, it only requires kindling to create in it an impulse to think independently and an ardent desire for the truth.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the idea to Plutarch’s Moralia and finds “no substantive evidence that Socrates” produced the saying.
The “kindling of a flame, not the filling of a vessel” wording was ascribed to Socrates in the Malaysian Journal of Education, June 1966 — the earliest such attribution QI located.
Plutarch’s line survives on Wikiquote as “The mind is not a vessel that needs filling, but wood that needs igniting” (Waterfield translation), with no Socrates credit.
A near-identical line, “Education is not the filling of a pail, but the lighting of a fire,” is separately misattributed to W. B. Yeats by the same paraphrase-drift mechanism.
source.excerptNote: Plutarch’s original thought, in the 1927 Loeb Classical Library rendering. Robin Waterfield’s 1992 Penguin version reads: “the correct analogy for the mind is not a vessel that needs filling, but wood that needs igniting.” Neither Plutarch nor his translators wrote the tidy “kindling of a flame… filling of a vessel” line now pinned on Socrates.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: The Mind Is Not a Vessel That Needs Filling

source.rightsNote: Plutarch’s original Greek is long in the public domain, but the exact popular English line — “Education is the kindling of a flame, not the filling of a vessel” — is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author or single source edition (first documented only in 1966), so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for it. The specific modern translations that carry the idea (Loeb 1927; Waterfield/Penguin 1992) are themselves under translators’ copyright.

author.name: Plutarch
author.heading: About Plutarch
author.metaLine: c. 46 – after 119 AD · Greek historian, biographer & philosopher
author.bio: Plutarch of Chaeronea was a Greek-born Roman-era essayist and biographer, best known for his Parallel Lives and the Moralia, a sprawling collection of ethical and philosophical essays. His essay “On Listening to Lectures” contains the image of the mind as wood to be kindled rather than a vessel to be filled — the true root of this famous ‘Socrates’ quote. He wrote roughly five centuries after Socrates lived.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable fake Socrates lines. Socrates left no writings, and nothing in Plato’s or Xenophon’s record of him contains it. The real thought belongs to Plutarch, several centuries later.

items.why: Quote Investigator found “no substantive evidence that Socrates” said this; the earliest Socrates credit is a 1966 journal, over two millennia after his death. Mass-quote sites like Goodreads still list it under Socrates with no source.
“Education is not the filling of a pail, but the lighting of a fire” is widely credited to Yeats but has never been found in his works; it stems from the same Plutarch passage.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine source is Plutarch’s Moralia, “On Listening to Lectures” — and even there the words are a translator’s, not the tidy slogan now sold as Socrates.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line endures because it captures a genuine educational ideal in one clean antithesis — learning as ignition, not storage. That elegance is exactly why it drifts onto Socrates: a maxim about the love of inquiry feels like it should belong to the philosopher who claimed to know only that he knew nothing.

But the polish is the tell. Plutarch’s actual sentence is longer and hedged with qualification; the slogan is a 20th-century compression that no ancient author wrote. Crediting it to Socrates gives a modern paraphrase a 2,400-year pedigree it never earned.
context.pull: Learning as ignition, not storage — a real idea, wrongly signed.
